did_you_know.text: The Hebrew verb for “holding oneself back” is connected with stopping or restraining emotion. Joseph can no longer hide how deeply moved he is.
“Plowing” means preparing the soil, while “harvest” means gathering the crops. The famine therefore prevents both planting and reaping.
“A father to Pharaoh” does not mean that Joseph was Pharaoh’s father. It is an expression of honor and authority, presenting Joseph as a senior adviser and leader.
The land of Goshen is usually identified with the eastern Nile Delta. It suited a large family that raised sheep and cattle and kept close to Joseph.
The Hebrew word here means wagons or carts, not young calves. They were meant to transport the children, women, and Jacob on the journey to Egypt.
In the ancient world, fine clothing was both a gift and a sign of honor and status. Benjamin receives five changes of clothes, showing Joseph’s special affection for him.
The verb “tirgazu” can relate to anger, agitation, or trembling. Joseph may therefore be warning his brothers not to quarrel or panic on the way.
The phrase “his heart failed him” describes sudden numbness or weakness, not simply a medical problem. Jacob struggles to believe news that is both reassuring and overwhelming.
Here Jacob is called “Israel,” a name that will later also refer to the nation. This family moment begins to connect with the national story of the Israelites.
